big_idea: Code is a list of instructions in ORDER.
learning_intention: We are learning to write step-by-step code for a simple task and follow it in order.
student_learning_goal: I can write step-by-step code for a simple task and follow it in order.
success_criteria: I can list 3 steps for a simple task in the correct order.
I can follow code instructions to move a robot on the grid.
I can write code that gets a robot from start to finish.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Coda the Coding Robot/illustration — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Per-pair set of code step cards
Lesson 1 sequence tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: How do you make a peanut-butter sandwich? Tell Coda STEP BY STEP. Coda opens with the unit refrain: 'STEP, by STEP, by STEP — that's CODE!' (Class echoes.)
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Reveal Coda the Coding Robot. 'Friends — meet Coda. Coda is a CODING ROBOT. Coda only does what we tell it — STEP by STEP. Today we'll write CODE for Coda.'

'Coda wants to make a peanut-butter sandwich. How does Coda do that?'

Take responses. Children might say: 'put peanut butter on bread'. 'OK — but Coda is VERY literal. What's the FIRST step?'

Lead them through:
Step 1: Get bread.
Step 2: Get peanut butter.
Step 3: Open peanut butter jar.
Step 4: Spread peanut butter on bread.
Step 5: Eat sandwich.

Write each step. 'This list is CODE. Each step is in ORDER. The first step is FIRST. The last step is LAST.'

'Now what happens if I CHANGE THE ORDER? What if step 4 came before step 3 — spread the peanut butter BEFORE opening the jar?' Children laugh. 'Doesn't work! The order MATTERS.'

Now grid mat. 'Coda also lives on a grid. We tell Coda to MOVE step by step.' Show the grid mat with Coda starting on the left edge. 'Code: Step 1 — move right. Step 2 — move right. Step 3 — move right. Where does Coda end up?' On the right side. 'Right. Now what if Step 2 was move UP instead?' Different ending position.

'Today we'll write code to move Coda around the grid.'
student_actions: List the steps to make a peanut-butter sandwich.
Discuss what happens when the order changes.
Predict where Coda lands after 3 'move right' steps.

steps.instruction: Whole group: code Coda's path on the grid. Start at (0,0). Code: right, right, up, up, right. Where does Coda end? (3, 2). Then change one step: replace the 5th 'right' with 'down'. Now where? (2, 1). Discuss how one change shifts the outcome.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Watch Coda follow the code. Predict the ending square BEFORE I move.' Slow down on each step.

steps.instruction: Send pairs to three stations (~7 min each). Station A: Code Coda's Path — pair has the grid mat, robot marker, and 5 step cards; they execute the code and find the ending square. Station B: Write the Path — pair has a starting and ending square; they write code (step cards) to get there. Station C: Real-Life Code — pair lists the steps for an everyday task (brushing teeth, walking to the bus stop) in 5+ steps.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Three stations, 7 minutes each.'

steps.instruction: Stretch challenge at Station B: include a path that requires turning (e.g., from (0,0) to (3,3)). Multiple correct codes — discuss alternative paths.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to pairs: 'Some paths can be coded MANY ways. Find at least 2 different codes for the same start-to-end.'

steps.instruction: Discuss order matters. 'Right, then up vs up, then right — same ending square. So order doesn't ALWAYS matter for movement.' But contrast: 'Spread peanut butter, then open jar' vs 'open jar, then spread' — order matters for sandwich making.
steps.teacher_prompt: Use both examples. Movement code is sometimes commutative; real-life code usually isn't.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the sequence tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask 'What's the first step? Last step?' Mark the tracker.

steps.instruction: STRATEGY COMPARE: 2 pairs share their step-by-step solutions for the same path. Pair A used 'forward, forward, turn, forward'; Pair B used 'forward 3 steps, turn, forward'. Class compares: which is more atomic? Which would Coda follow without confusion? Bers (2018) frames this as the discreteness principle — every command is one executable action.
steps.teacher_prompt: Coda: 'Same destination, different code. The MORE atomic the steps, the FEWER mistakes Coda makes.'

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. Use only 3-step codes with single direction (all rights, all ups).
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at Station B: include diagonal paths (right then up alternating). Discuss whether code can include diagonals.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide step cards with picture arrows. Sentence frame: 'First, ___. Then, ___.'
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Allow them to BE Coda — physically move on a large grid drawn on the floor.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: writes 3+ ordered steps for a task; executes code correctly on the grid; recognises that order matters.
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the sequence tracker per child.

discussion_prompts: Why does the ORDER of steps matter?
What happens if you swap two steps?
Can you give an example of code from your day?
Coda's preview: tomorrow Looper will show us how to SHORTEN our code with LOOPS (Lesson 2 — C3.1). What step-pattern in your code today REPEATED — that's the perfect candidate for tomorrow's loops.
consolidation.exit_routine: Coda's refrain — class chants three times together: "Coda says: STEP, by STEP, by STEP — that's CODE!" Each child writes ONE Coda command on a sticky and tags it with an action verb.

assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 1 is the diagnostic. Children at L4 articulate sequence as ORDERED steps.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child writes a 'jumble' of steps with no clear order — repairing the unordered-list error
expanded_walkthrough.rationale: Grade-1 children entering computational sequencing tasks frequently write narrative descriptions ('then he goes to the door') instead of discrete actions a robot can follow ('move 1 step, turn right, move 1 step'). The narrative-vs-action gap is well documented in early-CS research — Bers (2018) ScratchJr studies and the NRC (2011) Computational Thinking framework both place explicit, ordered, executable steps as the foundation of computational sequencing. Today we drill that explicitness so Lesson 2 (loops) can compress what they sequenced today, Lesson 3 (reading code) can decode it, and Lesson 4 (altering) can manipulate it.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station C. The child writes the sandwich code as 'spread, get bread, open jar, eat'. Out of order.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'Read your code aloud.' The child reads. 'Hmm — try doing it in that order. Spread BEFORE you have bread? Where does the peanut butter go?' The child laughs. 'Right — there's no bread yet.'

'Code MUST be in order. The first step has to be DOABLE first. What's the first thing Coda needs to make a sandwich?' 'Get bread.' 'Right. Number it 1.'

Walk through the order: 1. Get bread. 2. Get peanut butter. 3. Open jar. 4. Spread on bread. 5. Eat. 'See — each step BUILDS on the one before. That's SEQUENCE.'

If the child STILL writes unordered: physically act out the steps as the child reads. The mismatch between actions and order makes the issue visible.

Long-term recovery: every code-writing task uses NUMBERED steps. Trains the reflex.
expected_student_responses: (Strong) Numbers steps independently and explains why each comes when it does.
(Stretched) Writes code for harder tasks (cooking, building).
common_misconceptions: Order doesn't matter for code. (Repair: act out unordered code; the failure is visible.)
Code is just a description. (Children write narrative instead of steps. Repair: focus on EXECUTABLE actions.)
Code can skip steps. (Children leave out 'open jar'. Repair: every step needed must be in the code.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child writes narrative-not-actions ('he goes to the kitchen'): drop to physical 'finger-act each step' on a grid mat — child names ONE move per finger-tap, no narrative.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child writes complete actions but skips a step (jumps two squares): replay each step out loud as the child points; use a sentence frame 'first I ___, next I ___, next I ___'.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child includes turns inside moves ('walk and turn right'): explicitly separate by recasting on a card 'move 1 step. TURN right.' Drill turn-as-its-own-step until 5 commands are atomic.

parts_outline.task: Write 5 steps in order for a simple task (brush teeth, get dressed, walk to school).
Execute 4 grid codes — write the ending coordinate.
Open prompt: invent your own simple task. Write the code in 4-5 steps.
